intro: When a PDF on your Mac won't let you type, the form is usually locked, flat, or open in a viewer that cannot fill it. Preview can still place text for you with its Text Box tool, and that costs nothing. This page shows how to tell which problem you have, then which fix to try first.
tldr: Check the viewer first. Download the PDF and open it in Preview or Acrobat, not in a browser tab.
When a PDF won't accept typing, Preview's Text Box tool adds text on top of the page, as Apple's guide describes.
A creator who turned filling off, or a signature that locked the fields, needs to send you a new copy.
XFA forms do not work in Chrome's PDF viewer. Ask the sender for an AcroForm copy instead.

blocks.text: Check the file before you fight it
A blank field usually comes from a few causes, and each one has a different fix. Work through the checks in order. Start with the viewer, because a browser tab can hide fields that are really there.

Download the file to your Mac first. Open it from Downloads, not from a mail preview or a browser tab. Then answer one question: does the file have fields at all? You can answer that in a few minutes with Acrobat, or by clicking a field in Preview.

items: Open the file from Downloads, not from a browser tab or a mail preview.
In Acrobat, choose Tools > Prepare Form. A 'No form fields detected' message means the file has no fields.
In Acrobat, choose File > Properties > Security and read the line for filling form fields.
Check whether someone signed the file. A signature can lock the fields.

blocks.title: Looks fillable is not fillable
blocks.text: A form can have boxes, lines, and labels and still have no fields. Only real fields accept typing. Lines and boxes drawn on the page cannot take keystrokes, so you need a text tool instead.
How to fill out a PDF on Mac in Preview

Preview is the quickest route, and it ships with macOS. Right-click the file in Finder, then choose Open With > Preview. If the form has real fields, click into them and type. If nothing happens, the file may be flat or locked, so move on to the Text Box tool.

Apple's guide describes this exact case. It says: 'If a PDF won't allow you to type directly into the form, you can add a text box instead.' Use that route when the fields are missing or locked, and you still need to put words on the page.
Use the Text Box tool step by step

items: Open the PDF in Preview. Turn on the Markup toolbar if you do not see it.
Find the Text Box tool in the Form Filling Toolbar, the name Apple's guide uses.
Click the Text Box tool, then click the spot where the words should go.
Type your text. Drag the box to move it, and drag a corner to resize it.
Save with ⌘S, then close and reopen the file to confirm the text stayed.

blocks.title: AutoFill is not a guarantee
blocks.text: Preview's AutoFill does not work with every PDF. Apple's guide says 'Not all PDFs support this feature.' If AutoFill skips your form, the Text Box tool is the next step, not a sign the file is broken.
Why Acrobat blocks typing and how to check it

Acrobat has settings that can block filling. The first one to check is File > Properties > Security. AutoFillPDF's guide says a 'Not Allowed' next to Filling of form fields means the creator turned filling off. You cannot change that from your side, so ask the sender for a new copy.

Protected Mode is the other setting people blame. AutoFillPDF says it can stop keystrokes. Its fix is to clear 'Enable Protected Mode at startup' under Preferences > Security (Enhanced), restart Acrobat, and turn the setting back on afterward. Clear it only for a file you trust.

blocks.title: Turn Protected Mode back on
blocks.text: Clearing Protected Mode lowers Acrobat's security. Turn it back on once you have saved the form. Never clear it for a file from a sender you do not know.

The menu names in this section come from a third-party guide. Adobe's own help pages did not open during research for this page. Check the names against your Acrobat version, because newer releases may have moved them.
Why Chrome and XFA forms won't take typing

Chrome opens PDFs in its built-in viewer, which runs on PDFium. Datalogics says PDFium does not support XFA. XFA is a proprietary Adobe format for interactive forms. If the form is XFA, the fields may not respond in Chrome, even when they look ready.

Datalogics, in an article dated January 7, 2026, argues that ISO left XFA out of PDF 2.0 (ISO 32000-2:2017). It treats that as deprecation at the standards level. The article comes from a vendor and gives no Adobe end-of-support date for XFA in Acrobat Desktop. Read it as a warning, not a deadline.

If your form is XFA, the cleanest fix is an AcroForm copy from the sender. Datalogics calls converting to AcroForm 'the best long-term strategy' for forms that still need to be interactive. Ask for that version, and say the form must stay fillable.

blocks.text: What a PDF form you cannot type into costs you

The sources for this page do not count how often this problem happens, so no national figure appears here. What you can measure is your own time. Count the minutes lost to printing, scanning, and sending the form back. Compare that with the minutes it takes to ask for a fixed copy.

The closest measured figure comes from a study with 20 participants on PDF form remediation. They took a mean of 31 min 29 s to fix forms in Adobe Acrobat, and 12 min 55 s in a research tool called FormA11y. That study measured people preparing forms for accessibility, not people filling them in. It shows the work is slow when the tool fights you.

Paperwork at scale is large too. A Forbes article citing OMB says federal paperwork required 10.5 billion hours across 39 departments in FY2023. That total covers all federal forms, not PDFs alone. OMB's live inventory lists 12.3 billion, so the exact figure depends on the source you pick.

blocks.title: Regulated work needs extra care
blocks.text: If the form holds client, patient, or employee data, follow your employer's rules before you copy, scan, or paste it anywhere. That includes AI tools. Lawyers, nurses, and accountants should check those rules first.
Common mistakes that waste the most time

items: Printing to PDF to get around the block. A print often removes the fields, so you lose the ability to type later.
Editing the only copy. Save the sender's original, then fill a copy with a clear name.
Turning off Protected Mode and forgetting it. Turn it back on after you save.
Assuming a signed file can change. A signature can lock the fields.
Trusting the first result in Preview. A thread from around 2018 reports that editing fields turned text solid black.

blocks.text: That Apple Community thread dates from the High Sierra 10.13.3 era, and it has no confirmed cause or clean fix. Its reply says Preview is not a PDF editor. It recommends Adobe Acrobat Pro or a Mac App Store PDF editor, and it warns that forms using Acrobat JavaScript or LiveCycle may not work in Mac App Store editors. Test any tool on a copy first.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It can draw a circle and a label around a button, and it can guide you one click at a time. That helps when you cannot find the Text Box tool.

Lazur does not fill the form for you. It does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps. It is not a plugin for Preview or Acrobat. Dictation is the closest help for typing. Hold fn, speak, and Lazur types clean text at the cursor in any app. You still pick the field and check the words. If you want to try it, [download Lazur for your Mac](/download).

blocks.title: What Lazur sees
blocks.text: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. On client or patient data, follow your employer's rules first.
A routine for the next PDF that blocks you

Run the same checks in the same order each time. The plan above lists them. Keep a short note of which step solved each form, so the next one takes less time. Over a few forms, the pattern shows you which sender or viewer causes the most trouble.
What to ask the sender for
If the checks show a locked or XFA form, the sender holds the fix. A short, specific request works better than a vague one. Name the form, say you need to type into it, and list what needs to change.

items: A fillable AcroForm version, not an XFA form.
Filling enabled, with no Not Allowed setting for form fields.
An unsigned copy, or a copy from before the signature was added.
The editable source file, so they can export a fresh fillable PDF.

blocks.text: Save your filled copy under a clear name, and keep the original. If the form needs a signature, ask which signing method the recipient accepts. Then send the copy and keep a note of what you sent and when.

faq.question: Why won't my PDF let me type on Mac?
faq.answer: Most often the form has no fillable fields, the creator blocked filling, a signature locked the fields, or a browser viewer is in the way. Download the file and open it in Preview to test. If Preview still blocks typing, use the Text Box tool that Apple's guide describes.

faq.question: Can I fill out a PDF in Preview without buying Acrobat?
faq.answer: Often yes. Preview fills real fields and adds text boxes on flat PDFs. It has limits, though. A reply in an Apple Community thread says Preview is not a PDF editor, so forms with complex scripts may need another tool. Check the saved file before you send it.

faq.question: Why does the text turn solid black in Preview?
faq.answer: An Apple Community thread from around 2018 reports that editing or inserting fields turned text solid black. Acrobat DC showed the same behavior there. The thread does not confirm a cause. Test on a copy, check the output, and try the Text Box tool on a fresh download.

faq.question: Is it safe to turn off Protected Mode in Acrobat?
faq.answer: It lowers Acrobat's security, according to the AutoFillPDF guide that describes the setting. Turn it off only for a file you trust, restart, fill the form, then turn Protected Mode back on. Do not leave it off by habit.

faq.question: Does printing to PDF fix a form that won't take typing?
faq.answer: Usually not. A print to PDF often removes the fields, so you can no longer type into them. Keep the fillable original, and use the Text Box tool in Preview if you only need to add words to the page.

faq.question: What if the sender says the form is locked on purpose?
faq.answer: Ask what they need from the form. They may accept a printed copy that you fill by hand and scan, or a version with text boxes. Get their answer in writing, and keep your copy and their reply together.

faq.question: Does Lazur fill in the PDF for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur guides, points, explains, and drafts text. It does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. Hold fn to dictate text at the cursor, then choose the field and check the words yourself.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur on a form with client or patient data?
faq.answer: Check your employer's rules first. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and screenshots go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Follow your employer's policy before you use any AI tool on protected data.

costs.title: Time lost to workarounds
costs.text: Printing, scanning, and mailing the form back adds steps that a fillable file would skip. Each round trip with the sender adds delay. The fix is often one short request for a fillable copy, not an afternoon of workarounds.

costs.title: Wrong data from retyping
costs.text: When you retype values from a paper copy, typos creep in. A flat PDF with hand-placed text can look right while a value is off by one digit. Check every number after you place it, and compare it with the source.

costs.title: Damage to the original
costs.text: A print to PDF or a save over the sender's file can destroy the fields you needed. You then have no fillable copy to return. Keep the original untouched, and work on a copy with a clear name.

costs.title: Paying for software you may not need
costs.text: Full PDF editors can cost money. Check Adobe's pricing page before you buy anything. Try Preview first, since many blocked forms need only a text box for the words you must add.

costs.title: Compliance risk with sensitive data
costs.text: Pasting client, patient, or employee data into an unapproved tool can break your employer's rules. Check those rules before you scan, copy, or dictate any sensitive form.

causes.title: The creator turned filling off
causes.text: The author of the form can block filling in Acrobat. The setting sits under File > Properties > Security, where Filling of form fields can read Not Allowed. You cannot change that setting from your side, so the fix sits with the sender.

causes.title: A digital signature locked the fields
causes.text: AutoFillPDF lists a digital signature as a cause of fields that will not fill. Fields can stay locked to protect the signed content. If an unsigned version exists, ask for that copy instead.

causes.title: The file has no fields at all
causes.text: A flat PDF looks like a form but has no interactive fields. AutoFillPDF says that Tools > Prepare Form and a 'No form fields detected' message both point to this. Use the Text Box tool, or ask for a fillable copy.

causes.title: A browser viewer gets in the way
causes.text: AutoFillPDF names browser viewers as a common cause of fields that will not respond. It says Edge is especially weak for forms. Download the file and open it in Acrobat Reader or Preview to test the same form.

causes.title: XFA forms do not run in Chrome
causes.text: XFA is a proprietary Adobe format for interactive forms. Datalogics says Chrome's PDFium viewer does not support it. The fields can look like boxes that ignore keystrokes. Ask for an AcroForm copy, which Datalogics calls the best long-term option.

causes.title: Protected Mode or a damaged file
causes.text: AutoFillPDF says Acrobat's Protected Mode can stop keystrokes. It also lists a recent Acrobat update bug and corrupt files as causes. Adobe has not confirmed the update bug. Re-download the file and check Protected Mode before you assume the form is broken.

causes.title: Preview turns edited fields black
causes.text: An Apple Community thread reports that editing or inserting fields in Preview turned the text solid black. The same thread says Acrobat DC showed the same behavior. No cause was confirmed, so test on a copy and check the output before you send it.

fixes.title: Open the file in Preview first
fixes.text: Download the PDF, right-click it in Finder, and choose Open With > Preview. Click a field and type. Preview handles fillable AcroForm files, and it avoids the browser viewer. Save with ⌘S, then reopen the file to confirm the entries are still there.

fixes.title: Place text with the Text Box tool
fixes.text: Apple's guide says that if a PDF won't allow typing, you can add a text box instead. Turn on the Markup toolbar, choose the Text Box tool in the Form Filling Toolbar, click the spot, and type. It costs nothing, and it works where the form will not accept typing.

fixes.title: Clear Protected Mode, then restore it
fixes.text: In Acrobat, open Preferences > Security (Enhanced) and clear 'Enable Protected Mode at startup'. Restart, fill the form, and turn the setting back on. AutoFillPDF says clearing it lowers security, so use it only for files you trust.

fixes.title: Move the file out of the browser
fixes.text: Download the file and open it in Adobe's Acrobat Reader or in Preview. AutoFillPDF gives this as its fix for browser viewers. Avoid editing inside an email preview, since that adds one more viewer to the mix.

fixes.title: Ask for an AcroForm copy for XFA forms
fixes.text: Ask the sender for an AcroForm version. Datalogics calls that the best long-term strategy for forms that still need to be interactive. Do not print the XFA form to PDF, because a print usually removes the fields.

fixes.title: Ask for an unlocked, unsigned copy
fixes.text: Write a short request for a fillable copy with filling enabled and no signature lock. Name the pages that need text. Keep the reply, so you have a record of what the sender sent and when.

plan.label: Step 1
plan.title: Test the file in Preview
plan.text: Download the PDF to Downloads and open it in Preview. Browser tabs can hide or ignore fields, so this test catches a common cause quickly. If the field takes typing, you are done. If not, keep going.

plan.label: Step 2
plan.title: Check for real fields
plan.text: If you have Acrobat, choose Tools > Prepare Form. A 'No form fields detected' message means the file is flat. Without Acrobat, click where a field should be. If nothing responds, treat the file as flat and move on.

plan.label: Step 3
plan.title: Place text with Text Box
plan.text: Turn on the Markup toolbar, choose Text Box in the Form Filling Toolbar, click the spot, and type. Drag the box to move it and drag a corner to resize it. Save with ⌘S, then reopen the file and check it.

plan.label: Step 4
plan.title: Check the blocking settings
plan.text: In Acrobat, read File > Properties > Security. If filling is Not Allowed, the creator blocked it, and you need a new copy. If Protected Mode blocks keystrokes, clear it only for a file you trust, then turn it back on.

plan.label: Step 5
plan.title: Ask for a fixed copy
plan.text: Send a short request for a fillable AcroForm copy with filling enabled and no signature lock. Name the pages that need text. Keep the reply, so you have a record of what arrived and when.
